Sets

Problem 1. Given a linear space X, and its linear subspace V, then there is a linear subspace X of W, and X is the direct sum of V and W.

Proof. First we recall Zorn’s Lemma:

Lemma. Let X be a partially ordered non-empty set for which every totally ordered subset has an upper bound. Then X has a maximal element.

Let Γ denote the collection of all linear subspaces of X, all of which share with V only the 0 vector. It is trivial that zero space is in Γ, so it is not empty. Define a partial order ≺ as follows: Y1​≺Y2​ if Y1​⊂Y2​.

Now we verify that any totally ordered subset Γ′ of Γ has an upper bound. It suffices to show that Y′=⋃Y∈Γ′​Y is in Γ.

First, it is obvious that Y′∩V=∅.

Second, verify that Y′ is a linear subspace of X. For any y1​,y2​∈Y′ and scalar k, there is Y1​,Y2​∈Γ′, and yi​∈Yi​ (i=1,2). Since Γ′ is totally ordered, we could assume Y1​⊂Y2​. Then yi​∈Y2​, so y1​+y2​,ky1​∈Y2​⊂Y′, since Y2​ is a linear subspace of X.

Thus we could use Zorn’s Lemma to get a maximal element W of Γ. We will show that X=V⊕W. If it is not the case, there exists x in X, x cannot be decomposed as sum of vectors in V and W. Then let W′ denote the subspace generated by x,W, and W′∈Γ, contradicting to the maximality of W.

□

Problem 2. If A is countable, f:A→B is surjective, then B is countable.

Proof. Since f is surjective, then for any b∈B, the pre-image of b is non-empty. Choose g(b)∈f−1(b) arbitrarily for all b∈B, then g is injective. Thus B,g(B) are equipotent, but g(B)⊂A implies that g(B) is countable, then B is countable.

□

Problem 3. Suppose that A⊂R, for any x∈A, there is δ>0, such that(x−δ,x+δ)∩Ais countable. Then A is countable.

Proof. ∀x∈A,∃ ax​<x<bx​∈Q, with (ax​,bx​)∩A countable. Then: A=x∈A⋃​((ax​,bx​)∩A)⊂a<b∈Q,(a,b)∩A countable​⋃​(a,b)∩Ais countable since it is a subset of a countable union of countable sets.

□

Problem 4. Construct a bijection from R2 to R.

Proof. The readers are invited to surf the internet for answers.(Or can someone complete this?)

Hint: Consider the numbers in [0,1), and write them in decimals. Assume that we write the finite decimals NOT in the form of 0.XXX...XXX999..., but 0.XXX...XXX000...

Then we can "split" a number into two in the following way:

Example: 0.23989479837099981...

Write a bar after each number other than 9: 0.2∣3∣98∣94∣7∣98∣3∣7∣0∣9998∣1∣...

We have infinite many bars since there is no 0.XXX...XXX999...

Then we get two numbers: 0.2∣98∣7∣3∣0∣1∣... and 0.3∣94∣98∣7∣9998∣.... We can prove that this gives a bijection between [0,1) and [0,1)×[0,1) by writing its inverse (which is obvious).

□

Problem 6. Determine if it is true and give a proof: The collection of irrationals in [0,1], the decimal expansion of which contain no digit “7”, is Borel.

Proof. The following discussion is within [0,1] and using decimal expansion. Let A denote those numbers whose expansion contain digit “7”, then it suffices to check A is Borel. (Why?)

Let Bn​ denote numbers with the n-th position of expansion “7”, then Bn​ could be decomposed of countable disjoint intervals, thus it is Borel. Since A=⋃Bn​, A is also Borel.

□

Problem 9. Let C denote the collection of subsets of N that make this limit exist:n→∞lim​n∣A∩{1,⋯,n}∣​

And in case it exists, let p(A) denote it. Determine if (N,C,p) is a measure space.

Proof. In fact, the countable additivity is not satisfied.

First we construct a set A∈N, and the limit does not exist: A={j∈N,∃n∈Z+​,2n≤j<3×2n−1}

Then denote An​=∣A∩{1,⋯,n}∣, it is easy to observe: A3×2n−1​=k=1∑n​2k−1=2n−1,A2n−1​=2n−1−1n→∞lim​3×2n−1A3×2n−1​​=32​,n→∞lim​2n−1A2n−1​​=21​​

Which implies what we want. Then we seperate A into countable disjoint union of unit subsets. Each of them are in C, but A is not. A contradiction!

□

Problem 10. Assume (X,X,μ) to be a measure space, for any E1​,E2​∈X, we haveμ(E1​∪E2​)+μ(E1​∩E2​)=μ(E1​)+μ(E2​).

Proof. If the right hand side is infinity, then it is trivial.

Otherwise, due to countable additivity, we obtain ​μ(E1​∪E2​)=μ(E1​∩E2​)+μ(E1​−E2​)+μ(E2​−E1​)μ(E1​)=μ(E1​∩E2​)+μ(E1​−E2​)μ(E2​)=μ(E1​∩E2​)+μ(E2​−E1​)​

Which implies what we want.

□

Problem 11. Let E1​,E2​,⋯,En​ be Borel subsets of [0,1],∑k=1n​m(Ek​)>n−1, then ⋂k=1n​Ek​ is not empty.

Proof. Let Fk​=[0,1]\Ek​, then ⋂k=1n​Ek​=[0,1]\⋃k=1n​Fk​, which implies: m(k=1⋂n​Ek​)=1−m(k=1⋃n​Fk​)≥1−k=1∑n​m(Fk​)=1−k=1∑n​(1−m(Ek​))>0​

and it is obvious that ⋂k=1n​Ek​ is not empty.

□

Problem 12. (Poincaré Recurrence Theorem) Let (X,X,μ) be a probability space (a measure space with μ(X)=1), f:X→X is a measure-preserving transformation, which means: for any E measurable, f−1(E) is also measurable, and their measure coincide. Then for any set A of positive measure, there exists x∈A,n∈N+​, with f∘n(x)∈A.

Proof. We prove it by contradiction. If m(A)>0, but ∀x∈A,n∈N+​,f∘n(x)∈/A, then f∘n(A)∩A=∅, and we can easily prove by contradiction f∘(−n)(A)∩A=∅. Then again, A,f−1(A),⋯,f∘(−n)(A),⋯ are disjoint. Finally we obtain μ(n=1⋃∞​f∘(−n)(A))=n=1∑∞​μ(f∘(−n)(A))=n=1∑∞​μ(A)=∞

Contradicting to μ(X)=1!

□

Problem 13. ∀E⊂R,m∗(E)=inf{m∗(U),Uopen,E⊂U}

Proof. For any ε>0, let {Ik​} be a countable open cover of E, E⊂⋃Ik​,∑​m(Ik​)≤m∗(E)+ε.

Since U=⋃Ik​ is open, and E⊂U, we get: m∗(U)≤∑​m∗(Ik​)=∑​m(Ik​)≤m∗(E)+ε.

Using the definition of infimum, we are done.

□

Problem 14. If E,F⊂R with m∗(E△F)=0, where E△F=(E\F)∪(F\E). E is Lebesgue measurable if and only if F is Lebesgue measurable.

Proof. Due to the symmetry between E,F, we only deal with the case where E is measurable. Then for any T⊂R, we have: m∗(T)=m∗(T∩E)+m∗(T∩Ec).To prove F is measurable, it suffices to show: m∗(T)≥m∗(T∩F)+m∗(T∩Fc).

Then we observe and make use of the assumption: T∩F⊂(T∩E)∪(E△F),m∗(T∩F)≤m∗(T∩E)T∩Fc⊂(T∩Ec)∪(E△F),m∗(T∩Fc)≤m∗(T∩Ec)

Which implies what we want.

□

Problem 15. ∀A,B⊂R,m∗(A∪B)+m∗(A∩B)≤m∗(A)+m∗(B).

Proof. Using 13, we have ∀ε>0,∃U,V open, with: A⊂U,B⊂V,m∗(U)+m∗(V)<m∗(A)+m∗(B)+ε.

Since 10 holds for U,V, we obtain =​m∗(A∩B)+m∗(A∪B)≤m∗(U∩V)+m∗(U∪V)m∗(U)+m∗(V)<m∗(A)+m∗(B)+ε.​

Then we are done since ε is arbitrary.

□

Problem 16. Let d(A,B)>0, then m∗(A∪B)=m∗(A)+m∗(B).

Proof. If the right hand side is infinity, then it is trivial.

Otherwise, for any ε>0, let {Ik​} be a countable open cover of A∪B, ∑​m(Ik​)≤m∗(A∪B)+ε.

Since d(A,B)>0, we assume m(Ik​)<d(A,B), then {Ik​} cound be divided into two groups: {I1k​} covering A and {I2k​} covering B. So we have m∗(A)+m∗(B)≤∑​m(I1k​)+∑​m(I2k​)=∑​m(Ik​)≤m∗(A∪B)+ε.​

Then we are done since ε was arbitrary.

□

Problem 17. Assume m∗(E)<∞, and for any reals a<b,b−a=m∗((a,b)∩E)+m∗((a,b)\E).

Then E satisfies Caratheodory condition.

Proof. ∀T⊂R, our goal is to prove m∗(T)≥m∗(T∩E)+m∗(T∩Ec).

For any ε>0, let {Ik​} be a countable set of open intervals covering T, T⊂⋃Ik​,∑m(Ik​)≤m∗(T)+ε.

We obtain: T∩E⊂⋃(Ik​∩E),T∩Ec⊂⋃(Ik​∩Ec)m∗(T∩E)+m∗(T∩Ec)≤∑(m∗(Ik​∩E)+m∗(Ik​∩Ec))=∑m∗(Ik​)<m∗(T)+ε.​

Since ε was arbitrary, we are done.

□

Problem 22. Let f:R→R be pointwise differentiable, E⊂R,m(E)=0. Then m(f(E))=0.

Proof. We set En​={x∈E:∣f′(x)∣<n}, then f(En​) increases to f(E). Since m(E)=0, for any ε>0, there exists an open set U such that E⊂U and m(U)<ε/n.

For each x∈En​, there exsits a binary interval Jx​ such that x∈Jx​⊂U and m(f(Jx​))<nm(Jx​).

Then J={Jx​,x∈En​} is a cover of En​. By removing the duplicate parts we obtain J1​⊂J, a disjoint cover of En​. We have the estimate m(f(En​))≤∑m(f(Jx​))≤n∑m(Jx​)=nm(⋃Jx​)≤nm(U)<ε

Thus m(f(En​))=0 since ε was arbitrary. And finally m(f(E))=m(limf(En​))=limm(f(En​))=0.

□

Problem 23. Let f:R2→R be a continuous function. For any x∈R, let p(x) denote the number of y that satisfies f(x,y)=0. Then p(x) is Borel measurable.

Proof. Since p(x) is a positive integer-valued function, it suffices to prove {x:p(x)≥n} is borel for any positive integer n. Observe that {x:p(x)≥n}={x:∃ distinct y1​,⋯,yn​,f(x,yk​)=0}={x:∃N,m∈N+​,∃ distinct y1​,⋯,yn​,∣yk​∣≤N,∣yj​−yk​∣≥m1​,f(x,yk​)=0}=N=1⋃∞​m=1⋃∞​En​​

Where we denote En​={x:∃ distinct y1​,⋯,yn​,∣yk​∣≤N,∣yj​−yk​∣≥m1​,f(x,yk​)=0}

Thus our problem is reduced to prove En​ is closed. If so, it is Borel, then countable union of Borel sets is still Borel.

∀x0​∈En′​,∃{xr​}⊂En​,limxr​=x0​. since xr​∈En​, ∃yr1​,⋯,yrn​ pairwise disjoint, ∣yrk​∣≤N,∣yrj​−yrk​∣≥m1​,f(xr​,yrk​)=0.

Then for any r,k, yrk​ is bounded by N. Thus {(yr1​,⋯,yrn​)}⊂Rn is also bounded, and contains a subsequence {(yrt​1​,⋯,yrt​n​)} which converges to (y01​,⋯,y0n​). Still we have ∣y0k​∣≤N,∣y0j​−y0k​∣≥m1​, and since f is continuous, we obtain f(x0​,y0k​)=f(lim(xrt​​,yrt​k​))=limf(xrt​​,yrt​k​)=0.

Finally x0​ is in En​. Thus En​ is closed.

□

Problem 24. Let μ be a Borel measure on R. Then real-valued functionf(x)=r→0liminf​rμ((x−r,x+r))​

is Borel measuable.

Proof. Since f(x)=limr0​→0+​fr0​​(x), where we denote fr0​​(x)=0<r<r0​inf​rμ((x−r,x+r))​.

It is obvious that for a fixed x, the function fr0​​(x) of r0​ is decreasing. Thus we obtain f(x)=supf1/n​(x). Next we shall prove this f1/n​(x) is Borel measurable, then the supremum of it is still Borel measurable.

We claim that for any n∈N+​,c∈R, the set {f1/n​(x)<c} is open.

For any x0​∈{f1/n​(x)<c}, we have {f1/n​(x0​)<c}. Using definition, there exists 0<r<1/n, such that μ((x0​−r,x0​+r))<cr. Thus take one more 0<s≪r, such that μ((x0​−r,x0​+r))<c(r−s).

For any x∈U(x0​,s), we have U(x,r−s)⊂U(x0​,r). Then μ((x−(r−s),x+(r−s)))≤μ((x0​−r,x0​+r))<c(r−s)0<r<n1​inf​rμ((x−r,x+r))​≤r−sμ((x−(r−s),x+(r−s)))​<cThus f1/n​(x)<c, namely U(x0​,s)⊂{f1/n​(x)<c}, so it is open, then Borel measurable.

□

Problem 26. Suppose {fn​}1∞​⊂L+,fn​→f pointwise, and ∫f=lim∫fn​<∞. Then ∫E​f=lim∫E​fn​ ∀E∈M. However, this need not be true if ∫f=limfn​=∞.

Proof. *:Applying Fatou Lemma to the complement of E.

Let E∈M and ∫f<∞, we have: ∫f=∫(χE​f+χEc​f)=∫χE​f+∫χEc​fAnd similarly for substituting fn​ for f above. Now, since fn​→f⇒χF​fn​→χF​f,∀F∈M, we may apply Fatou’s Lemma as follows: ∫E​f=∫n→∞liminf​χE​fn​≤n→∞liminf​∫E​fn​=∗n→∞liminf​(∫fn​−∫Ec​fn​)=∗∗∫f−n→∞limsup​∫Ec​fn​Where we have =∗ since ∫E​f=∫χE​f+∫χEc​f, and =∗∗ since liminf∫fn​=lim∫fn​=∫f and liminf−∫g=−limsup∫g. However, since all terms above are finite, we may gain by apply Fatou’s Lemma (and in noticing the similarity to the steps made above) to see that: n→∞limsup​∫Ec​fn​=n→∞limsup​(∫fn​−∫E​fn​)=∫f−n→∞liminf​∫E​fn​≤∫f−∫E​f.And thus by substituting this in, we have: ∫E​f≤n→∞liminf​∫E​fn​≤n→∞limsup​∫E​fn​≤∫E​f.And therefore all the inequalities in the equation(s) above are actually equalities, and so we have: n→∞liminf​∫E​fn​=n→∞limsup​∫E​fn​=n→∞lim​∫E​f=∫E​f.We now turn our attention showing the above result need not hold if ∫f=lim∫f=∞ by means of a counter-example. Let E=(0,1],f=χ[2,∞)​, and fn​=χ[2,∞)​+nχ(0,1/n]​. Then fn​→f p.w., and: ∫(0,1]​fn​=nμ((0,1/n])=1∀n∈N⇒n→∞lim​∫(0,1]​fn​=1.However, ∫(0,1]​f=0, thus ∫E​f=lim∫E​fn​ need not be true if lim∫fn​=∫f=∞.

Problem 27. Suppose that {fj​} is a sequence in L1 such that ∑1∞​∫j​∣fj​∣<∞. Then ∑1∞​fj​ converges a.e. to a function in L1, and ∫∑1∞​fj​=∑1∞​∫fj​.

Proof. ∫∑1∞​∣fj​∣=∑1∞​∫∣fj​∣<∞, so the function g= ∑1∞​∣fj​∣ is in L1. In particular, ∑1∞​∣fj​(x)∣ is finite for a.e. x, and for each such x the series ∑1∞​fj​(x) converges. Moreover, ∣∑1n​fj​∣≤g for all n, so we can apply the dominated convergence theorem to the sequence of partial sums to obtain ∫∑1∞​fj​=∑1∞​∫fj​.

□

Problem 32. Let μ(X)<∞,f:X→[0,∞) be bounded. Then∫​fdμ=inf{∫​φdμ:φ≥f,φ simple}Moreover, prove by examples that the condition μ(X)<∞ is necessary.

Problem 42. Let fn​ be a sequence of non-negative Borel measurable functions on [0,1] that converges to f a.e. Moreover, we have∫01​fn​(x)log(fn​(x)+2)dx≤1.

Thus ∫E​∣x−y∣21​dy≥δ1​→∞ as δ→0,a contradiction to Fubini’s theorem since Lebesgue density points also have positive measure.

Problem 44. Let f:R→R be Lebesgue integrable. Then for x∈R a.e. the series converges:n=1∑∞​n​1​f(x−n​).

where I is a close interval with end points x,x0​.

Problem 47. Let f:R→R be monotone increasing, E⊂R is Lebesgue measurable, For any ε>0, there exists a sequence of open intervals (ai​,bi​), such thatE⊂⋃(ai​,bi​),∑∣f(bi​)−f(ai​)∣<ε

Problem 48. Let f:[0,1]→[0,1] be a continuous bijection, but not absolutely continuous. Then there exists E⊂[0,1], such that m(E)=0,m(f(E))>0.

Proof. First we prove two lemmas.

Lemma. Let f be differentiable on E⊂R, and ∣f′∣≤M on E, then m∗(f(E))≤Mm∗(E).

Proof. It is a more general case of 22, thus can be proved in a similar way.

□

Lemma. Let f be measurable on [a,b], E⊂[a,b] is measurable, and f is differentiable everywhere on E, then m∗(f(E))≤∫E​∣f′∣.

Proof. For each ε>0, denote Ek​={x∈E:(k−1)ε≤∣f′∣<kε}, by the first lemma we have m∗(f(Ek​))≤kεm(Ek​)=(k−1)εm(Ek​)+εm(Ek​)≤∫Ek​​∣f′∣+εm(Ek​)

Add them together, we obtain m∗(f(E))≤∫E​∣f′∣+εm(E), then we are done since ε was arbitrary.

□

Back to our proof, we will first show f∈BV from continuous and bijective property. Then by assuming the conclusion is false, we will prove f∈AC, a contradiction.

We have two approaches to prove f∈BV. One is that f is monotone as a continuous bijection. The other one can deal with more general cases.

∀0=x0​<x1​<⋯<xn​=1, we denote Jk​ as the close interval with endpoints f(xk−1​),f(xk​). Then by continuity, we have Jk​⊂f([xk−1​,xk​])=Ik​. Thus k=1∑n​∣f(xk​)−f(xk−1​)∣=∫01​k=1∑n​χJk​​dy≤∫01​k=1∑n​χIk​​dy≤1

Where we used the bijective property. In fact, even not being bijective our conclusion f∈BV still holds as long as the number of every point’s preimage is bounded by a same number.

Now assume f preserves zero measure. By f∈BV we know f′ exists a.e. and it is integrable. Hence there exists E⊂[0,1] such that m(E)=0 and f′ exists everywhere in [0,1]\E. By the assumption, m(f(E))=0. We observe that ∀(x,y)⊂[0,1],∣f(y)−f(x)∣≤m(f([x,y]))≤m∗(f([x,y]\E))+m(f(E))≤∫xy​∣f′(t)∣dt, the last inequality by the second lemma.

Now we make use of the integrablility of f′ and the absolute continuity of Lebesgue integral, for any ε>0, there exists δ>0, ∫A​∣f′∣<ε as long as m(A)<δ.

Finally we check the definition of absolute continuity of f. For each ε>0, for any 0≤a1​<b1​<⋯<an​<bn​≤1 with ∑(bk​−ak​)<δ, we have k=1∑n​∣f(bk​)−f(ak​)∣≤k=1∑n​∫ak​bk​​∣f′∣=∫⋃k=1n​(ak​,bk​)​∣f′∣<ε.

□

Problem 53. Let 1≤p<∞, fn​,f∈Lp, and fn​→f a.e. Then ∥fn​−f∥p​→0⇔∥fn​∥p​→∥f∥p​.

Proof. If ∥fn​−f∥p​→0, then ∣∥fn​∥p​−∥f∥p​∣≤∥fn​−f∥p​→0, thus ∥fn​∥p​→∥f∥p​.

The right-hand side converges to ∣f∣p a.e. and its integral also converges to the integral of ∣f∣p, thus by DCT we have ∫​∣∣​2fn​−f​∣∣​p→∫​0=0,

Problem 58. Let f:R→R be a Lebesgue measurable bijection, and f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y), then f is continuous.

Proof. Using Lusin’s theorem, there exists a compact K⊂[0,1] such that m(K)>2/3 and f continuous on K. Let ε>0. In fact, f is uniformly continuous on K, so there exists δ>0 such that ∣x−y∣<δ implies ∣f(x)−f(y)∣<ε ; without loss of generality, suppose δ<1/3.

Let 0<h<δ. Notice that the intersection between K and K−h is nonempty; otherwise 1+h=μ([−h,1])≥μ(K∪K−h)=μ(K)+μ(K−h)=2μ(K)>4/3

So h>1/3 whereas h<δ<1/3 by assumption.

Let x0​∈K∩(K−h). We have ∣f(x0​+h)−f(x0​)∣<ε, hence ∣f(h)∣<ε because f is additive. You deduce that f is continuous at 0.

Finally, it is straightforward to conclude that f is continuous on R.

Problem 60. Let H be the set of every absolutely continuous functions f:[0,1]→R that satisfies∥f∥H​:=∥f∥2​+∥f′∥2​<∞.

Then (H,∥⋅∥H​) is Banach space.

Proof. It is obvious that ∥⋅∥H​ is a norm. Then it suffices to check any Cauchy sequence converges to some point in H.

If fn​ is Cauchy in H, then fn​ and fn′​ are both Cauchy in L2([0,1]). Thus we assume fn​→f,fn′​→g in L2([0,1]). To show fn​→f in H, we must check f′=g a.e.

Since fn​∈AC, we have fn​(x)=fn​(0)+∫0x​fn′​(t)dt

In the following we will deduce f(x)=f(0)+∫0x​g(t)dt from it, which implies f′=g a.e.

Since fn​→f in L2([0,1]), we have a subsequence fnk​​→f a.e.

By Holder’s inequality we have ∣∣​∫0x​fn′​(t)dt−∫0x​g(t)dt∣∣​≤x​∫0x​(fn′​(t)−g(t))2dt→0

Thus we are done by taking the limit in the subsequence.

□

Problem 61. Let f:R→R be a Lebesgue integrable, and for any φ:R→R such that φ≥0 is bounded and continuous, we have ∫φf≥0. Then f≥0 a.e.

Proof. If f<0 on E with m(E)>0, then ∫E​f=−A<0, where A>0.

By the absolutely continuity of the integral of ∣f∣, ∃δ>0, and ∫T​∣f∣<A/2 as long as m(T)<δ.

Using Lusin’s theorem, there exists h:R→[0,1] continuous, such that for F={h=χE​}, we have m(F)<δ. Then ∣∫(h−χE​)f∣≤∫F​∣f∣<A/2. Hence ∫hf=∫(h−χE​)f+∫χE​<A/2+(−A)=−A/2<0.

□

Problem 62. Let fn​∈L2([0,1]), and constants A,B such that for each n, the following holds:0<A<∥fn​∥1​≤∥fn​∥2​<B.

Let a sequence of non-negative reals cn​ such that for F(x)=∑1∞​∣cn​fn​(x)∣, we have F(x)<∞ a.e. Denote En​={F(x)>n}, prove the following:

limn→∞​m(En​)=0.

∫En​​∣fk​(x)∣dx≤Bm(En​)​.

∑1∞​ck​<∞.

Proof. (1) limn→∞​m(En​)=m(⋂n=1∞​En​)=m({F(x)=∞})=0.

(2) ∫En​​∣fk​∣≤(∫En​​∣fk​∣2)21​(∫En​​12)21​≤∥f∥2​m(En​)​≤Bm(En​)​.

(3) From (2) we know that ∫Enc​​∣fk​(x)∣dx≥A−Bm(En​)​.

Now sum the above inequalities over all k≥1 with weights ck​. This leads to the following:∫Enc​​∣F(x)∣dx≥2A​k≥1∑​ck​.But the left hand side is finite according to the choice of En​, so k≥1∑​ck​<∞.

Problem 63. Let F be a nonempty set of some Lebesgue integrable functions on R that satisfies the following:

•

If f,g∈F, set h(x)=max(f(x),g(x)), then h∈F.

•

M=sup{∫R​f(x)dx}<∞.

Then there exists φ such that the following holds:

•

For any f∈F, f≤φ holds a.e.

•

∫R​φ=M.

Proof. Select a sequence {fn​} in F such that ∫fn​→M. Then let gn​=max(f1​,⋯,fn​), and φ=supfn​, we have for any fixed x, gn​(x) increases to φ(x). Thus lim∫gn​=∫φ. But on one hand gn​∈F⇒∫gn​≤M⇒lim∫gn​≤M, on the other hand gn​≥fn​⇒lim∫gn​≥lim∫fn​=M. Thus ∫φ=M.

If there is some f∈F such that f>φ on a positive measure, consider hn​=max(gn​,f)∈F.

By the constructions above, (hn​)n≥1​ is an increasing sequence of functions and thus converges pointwise to a function h.

Since by the given condition that ∫hn​≤M and the fact that hn​≥h1​ where h1​ is integrable, the monotone convergence theorem holds for (hn​)n≥1​ and thus ∫h≤M.

However, h>φ on a positive measure and h≥φ everywhere. These imply that M≥∫h>∫φ=M,which is absurd.

(Proof by contradiction is not necessary, but it is shorter.)

□

Problem 64. Let A=(aij​)1≤i,j≤n​ be an n−order real square symmetric matrix, and f(x1​,x2​,⋯,xn​)=exp(−∑j,k=1n​xjk​aj​ak​).

1.

Prove that f∈L1(Rn) iff A is positive definite.

2.

Assuming A is positive definite, compute ∫Rn​f(x)dx.

Proof.

1.

Since A is real and symmetric, it can be orthogonal diagonalized. Assume Q is orthogonal with detQ=1, such that QAQ−1=D=diag{λ1​,λ2​,⋯,λn​}, where each λi​ is an eigenvalue of A.

Then f(x)=exp(−xTAx)=exp(−xTQTDQx)=exp(−yTDy), where we denote y=Qx.

Thus ∫Rn​f(x)dx=∫Rn​exp(−yTDy)dx=∫Rn​exp(−yTDy)dy=∫Rn​exp(−k=1∑n​λk​yk2​)dy1​⋯dyn​.

Therefore, f∈L1(Rn) iff ∀i=1,2,⋯n,λi​>0 iff A is positive definite.

2.

By the above discussions, using Tonelli’s theorem we have ∫Rn​f(x)dx=∫Rn​exp(−k=1∑n​λk​yk2​)dy1​⋯dyn​=k=1∏n​∫R​exp(−λk​t2)dt=detAπn​​.

□
